newsitem.title: UK: Bruised European stocks brace for more pain Monday.
newsitem.headline: Bruised European stocks brace for more pain Monday.

text.p: Battered European stocks are set for fresh pain on Monday as the shock of last week's historic Wall Street tumble sinks in, analysts said.
The Dow Jones industrial average suffered its second biggest point loss ever on Friday, sliding 247.37 points or 3.11 percent to close at 7,694.66.

The Dutch AEX index slumped 4.4 percent, while Germany's DAX ended electronic trading with a 2.8 percent loss and Britain's FTSE 100 index fell 2.5 percent -- its heftiest percentage drop since October 1992.
French and Italian markets were spared as they were closed on Friday for Assumption Day, but they are set to feel the pinch on Monday, analysts said.
"The market is definitely going to open down, around one percent," said Olivier Blitz, head of equity sales at IFF Bourse in Paris. "The market is very much following the Dow."
The Paris bourse closed on Thursday down 2.48 percent at 2,921.84. Blitz predicted France's CAC 40 index would consolidate down to strong technical support around 2,850 and below there at 2,830.
In Milan, one senior broker foresaw an initial -- but brief -- period of quiet as the Italian market struggled to absorb the events of Friday.

"Once they've thought it out it'll have a negative effect. It wouldn't be impossible to see an intraday fall of three percent," he said, though he thought it likely Italian shares would recover later to close around one percent lower.
Italy's blue-chip Mib30 index finished 0.05 percent stronger on Thursday, ahead of the holiday weekend, at 21,756.
Germany's Welt am Sonntag newspaper warned of market mayhem in the making, splashing the headline "Black Monday threatens stock market" on its front page on Sunday.

It quoted analysts predicting big losses both in New York and Frankfurt. Volker Bien, an equity analyst at BHF Bank in Frankfurt, told the paper the Dow could skid down to 7,200 in coming trading sessions.
Matthias Barz, a securities trader at UBS, saw the DAX falling to between 3,800 and 3,900 from Friday's close of 4,152.86.
Concerns over U.S. corporate earnings and a drop in the dollar took their toll on the Dow and its fellows last week.
Analysts said markets would remain jittery as they awaited Tuesday's meeting of the Federal Reserve Open Market committee, which will determine the fate of U.S. interest rates.
Germany's Bundesbank will also set monetary policy next week, when it reconvenes on Thursday after a summer break.
But some analysts sounded a reassuring note.

"It's quite often the case that when investors have the weekend to think about things, they don't react as vigorously as they might have done had it been an overnight move," said Richard Jeffrey, economist at Charterhouse Tilney in London.
"I think market-makers will mark the market down reasonably sharply first thing on Monday, probably by another 50 points or so, and then there will be a pause," he said.
The FTSE 100 index ended on Friday at 4,866 -- a far cry from the all-time high of 5,095.3 it hit as recently as August 7 -- and some market-watchers smelled a buying opportunity.
"At 5,100, cash was looking a safer bet," said Robert Buckland, UK stock strategist at HSBC James Capel here. "But at these levels I'll pick up the phone and advise clients to get back into stocks."
